question: What is the traditional 'golden period' for primary closure of a clean, uninfected laceration?
explanation: Closing a clean wound within six to eight hours minimizes bacterial proliferation before the tissue host defenses become overwhelmed. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why can facial and scalp lacerations often be closed safely outside the standard time window for primary closure?

options.A: Sweat glands in the head naturally secrete natural antibacterial agents
options.B: The abundant vascular supply enhances local tissue resistance and healing
options.C: These regions have lower exposure to environmental pathogens
options.D: The skin in these areas is much thinner and easier to approximate

explanation: High vascularity delivers high concentrations of oxygen, nutrients, and white blood cells, which drastically reduce the likelihood of wound infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h1)

question: When must the neurovascular status distal to a wound be assessed and documented?

options.A: Only when the patient complains of numbness
options.B: Immediately after placing the final suture
options.D: During the dressing change forty-eight hours later

explanation: Local anesthetics temporarily block nerve conduction, making it impossible to accurately assess baseline nerve function if testing is delayed until afterward. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h2)

question: A patient presents with a deep glass-cut on the palm. What is a vital diagnostic step before proceeding to local infiltration and suturing?

options.A: Performing a complete blood count and coagulation profile
options.B: Irrigating the wound with high-pressure hydrogen peroxide
options.C: Testing motor movement and two-point discrimination distal to the cut

explanation: Palmar lacerations frequently involve underlying digital nerves and flexor tendons, which must be identified prior to closure. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which anatomical areas should NOT receive a local anesthetic containing epinephrine?
explanation: End-arterial beds lack collateral circulation, making them vulnerable to terminal ischemia and tissue necrosis when exposed to epinephrine-induced vasoconstriction. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary pharmacological advantage of adding epinephrine to a local anesthetic solution?

options.A: It neutralizes the acidic pH of the tissue, eliminating the burning sensation
options.B: It permanently alters nerve receptor sites to prevent future pain transmission
options.C: It causes local vasoconstriction, reducing bleeding and prolonging anesthesia duration
options.D: It accelerates the chemical breakdown of bacteria inside the wound bed

explanation: Constricting local blood vessels keeps the anesthetic agent localized around the nerve fibers longer while simultaneously providing a clearer surgical field. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which solution is generally preferred for irrigating traumatic wounds in the emergency setting?
explanation: Normal saline is an isotonic fluid that effectively cleanses the wound without harming exposed cellular structures or delaying healing. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why is the routine use of hydrogen peroxide discouraged for irrigating deep emergency wounds?

options.A: It is cytotoxic to healthy tissue and damages newly forming cells
options.B: It neutralizes the effectiveness of any local anesthetic already given
options.C: It permanently stains the surrounding skin a bright yellow-orange
options.D: It causes immediate systemic hypotension and profound bradycardia

explanation: The vigorous bubbling action of hydrogen peroxide destroys fragile granulation tissue and impairs local cellular immunity, increasing infection risk. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which property distinguishes a monofilament suture from a multifilament suture?

options.A: It elicits a much higher inflammatory response in skin
options.B: It is always classified as absorbable by the manufacturer
options.C: It requires specialized knots that cannot be tied by hand
options.D: It is composed of a single solid strand of material

explanation: Monofilament sutures consist of a single strand, which offers less resistance through tissue and harbors fewer bacteria compared to braided multifilaments. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: When should a cutting needle be selected over a tapered needle during emergency wound repair?

options.B: When closing deep subcutaneous fat layers
options.C: When closing tough, fibrous skin layers
options.D: When suturing highly delicate blood vessels

explanation: Skin has high tensile strength and requires the sharp cutting edge of a cutting needle to pass smoothly through the dermis without bending. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary advantage of using simple interrupted sutures for most emergency lacerations?

options.A: If one suture fails or becomes infected, the remaining sutures keep the wound secure
options.B: They eliminate the need for any subsequent suture removal appointments
options.C: They can be left in place indefinitely without causing skin irritation
options.D: They require significantly less suture material than any other technique

explanation: Because each interrupted stitch is tied off individually, failure of one unit does not compromise the stability of the entire repair. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why is skin edge eversion critical when placing epidermal sutures?

options.A: It allows the wound to heal entirely without forming any fibrous tissue
options.B: It accelerates the absorption rate of non-absorbable nylon material
options.C: It prevents a depressed or sunken scar as the wound heals and contracts
options.D: It completely eliminates the requirement for deep dermal support stitches

explanation: Wounds naturally flatten and contract over time; everting the edges ensures they do not pull inward, which creates an unsightly, depressed scar line. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the standard timeframe for removing facial sutures to minimize permanent stitch marks?
explanation: Facial skin heals rapidly and is vulnerable to cross-hatching or track marks if non-absorbable sutures are left in place too long. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h7)

question: Which symptom reported by a patient during a follow-up call is most indicative of a developing wound infection?

options.A: Spreading redness and increasing throbbing pain around the edges
options.B: Slight itching as the epidermal layers begin to knit together
options.C: A small amount of dried blood crusting over the knot
options.D: A mild pink discoloration directly adjacent to the suture line

explanation: Expanding erythema, warmth, and worsening pain are classic clinical signs of bacterial proliferation overcoming local tissue defenses. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the term for the partial or total separation of wound edges after surgical closure?
explanation: Dehiscence refers to the bursting open or splitting apart of a wound along the surgical suture line. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h8)

question: A patient with an uncertain tetanus vaccination history presents with a deep, dirty puncture wound from a rusty farm tool in a rural Nigerian clinic. What immediate interventions are required?

options.A: Immediate primary closure of the wound without checking immunization history
options.B: Only a course of oral analgesics and a sterile dry pressure dressing
options.C: Administration of intravenous broad-spectrum antifungal medications
options.D: Administration of both a tetanus toxoid vaccine and tetanus immune globulin

explanation: Tetanus-prone wounds in patients with unknown or incomplete immunization require passive immunity via immune globulin alongside active immunization with the toxoid. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h8)
